intro: A witches’ sabbath ends at the sound of a village church bell. Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1886 concert version sends racing violins and threatening brass into a long, unexpectedly tender dawn.

sections.label: A · Racing violins, brass summons
sections.mNote: Allegro feroce begins with the two violin sections alone

sections.label: B · Short wind and string dances
sections.mNote: Detached figures pass between woodwinds and strings

sections.label: C · Long phrases over muted violins
sections.mNote: The woodwinds sustain their tune above repeated string figures

sections.label: A′ · The brass summons returns
sections.mNote: Quick string figures meet the opening’s heavy brass answers

sections.label: D · A bell disperses the witches
sections.mNote: A bell in D sounds above quiet strings

sections.label: Coda · Clarinet and flute at daybreak
sections.mNote: Solo woodwinds sing above low strings and harp

relations.label: The opening agitation returns
relations.basis: In Rimsky-Korsakov’s concert version, opening fast material returns after contrasting episodes; these excerpts link the opening with the renewed-pressure section marked near 365 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.924, sustained 15.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 343.5 s (cache/form/mussorgsky-night-bald-mountain.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Violins in the dark
cues.text: The two violin sections begin alone, pianissimo, their quick figures circling around one another. Allegro feroce: fast and ferocious. Low strings soon tap out a pulse beneath them, and flute and oboe add their first held notes.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov’s concert score, Bessel edition, p. 3, first four bars: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP139196-PMLP04739-Mussorgsky_-_Night_on_Bald_Mountain_FS_rsl.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Borodin meets the young officer
cues.text: Autumn 1856, a Saint Petersburg military hospital: the army doctor Borodin, on duty, meets the seventeen-year-old Guards officer Mussorgsky. That evening, in a close-fitting uniform, with pomaded hair and immaculate nails, Mussorgsky plays extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata. In 1858 he petitions to leave the army.
cues.evidence: Borodin’s own account of the meeting, in the hospital duty room and that evening at the chief physician’s house, is quoted in Georgy Khubov’s biography of Mussorgsky, ch. 3 (Russian; translation ours): http://mussorgsky.ru/hubov019.html . The petition to leave the regiment is dated 1 May 1858 in Istoriya russkoy muzyki, vol. 7, Mussorgsky chapter: https://lib.rmvoz.ru/bigzal/irm/7/musorgskij/st

cues.title: A night for Chernobog
cues.text: The printed programme conjures underground voices, spirits of darkness and Chernobog, the Black God. His followers celebrate a black mass and a sabbath. A distant village church bell breaks up the gathering; day returns.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 2, Russian and French programme printed with Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1886 preface.

cues.title: A sinful prank
cues.text: In July 1867, weeks after finishing the score, Mussorgsky tells the literary scholar Vladimir Nikolsky that he sees in this “sinful prank” an original Russian work, nourished on Russian bread. Balakirev rejects it and will not have it performed. Mussorgsky keeps returning to the music, recasting it for the stage.
cues.evidence: Mussorgsky to V. V. Nikolsky, Minkino, 12 July 1867 (“sinful prank”, “nourished on Russian bread”: our translation of the Russian), quoted in Istoriya russkoy muzyki, vol. 7, note 73: https://lib.rmvoz.ru/bigzal/irm/7/musorgskij/st . Balakirev’s refusal to perform the piece at the Free Music School: https://www.belcanto.ru/mussorgsky_night.html . Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, p. 220, on Balakirev’s criticism and the versions for Mlada and The Fair at Sorochyntsy: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.title: Rimsky-Korsakov at the desk
cues.text: Saint Petersburg, 1886. Five years after Mussorgsky’s death, Rimsky-Korsakov assembles this concert piece from his friend’s manuscripts. Much of it comes through the later choral version for The Fair at Sorochyntsi. The witches now have a score ready for the concert hall.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov dates his preface Saint Petersburg, 1886, in the Bessel score, p. 2. The Sorochyntsi source and recomposition are discussed at https://www.laphil.com/works/night-on-bald-mountain

cues.title: The village bell
cues.text: A bell tuned to D rings through the dispersing dance. The score slows to Poco meno mosso; the violins tremble quietly and the cellos pluck D. Brass and percussion that drove the sabbath fall silent.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 60, rehearsal W: Campana in D, Poco meno mosso, quiet violin tremolo and pizzicato cellos on D; trombones, tuba, bass drum and cymbals cease.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A bell the hall could not tune
cues.text: In Mussorgsky’s last version, for his opera The Fair at Sorochyntsi, the sabbath is a sleeping peasant lad’s dream and a village bell dispels it. At the 1886 première, the bell Rimsky-Korsakov chooses at the bell-store goes off pitch in the hall as the temperature changes. A tam-tam takes its place.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life (Joffe translation), p. 221: in the version for The Fair at Sorochyntsy the peasant lad sees the witches’ sabbath in a dream and the piece ends with the ringing of the village church bell. P. 236, on the first Russian Symphony Concert of the 1886–87 season: “Only a tamtam had to be substituted for the bell”, the one he chose at the bell-store being off pitch in the hall “owing to a change in temperature”. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.title: A clarinet at dawn
cues.text: Meno mosso, tranquillo. A solo clarinet sings dolce, sweetly, above divided violas and low strings. The violins are silent. D remains in the bass while the clarinet’s little turns wander overhead.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 64, rehearsal Y: Meno mosso, Tranquillo, solo clarinet marked dolce, divided violas, cellos and double basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The flute’s answering phrase
cues.text: A solo flute takes the next phrase, also marked dolce. The double basses pluck their low notes while divided violas and cellos sustain the harmony. The flute’s last notes die away.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 64, rehearsal Z: solo flute marked dolce and perdendosi, divided violas, bowed cellos and pizzicato double basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repin in the hospital
cues.text: In March 1881 Ilya Repin paints Mussorgsky in the Nikolaevsky Military Hospital in Saint Petersburg: four sittings, the sitter in a hospital robe with crimson lapels. Mussorgsky dies there on 28 March, a week after his forty-second birthday.
cues.evidence: The Tretyakov Gallery, which owns the portrait, says Repin came to the Nikolaevsky Military Hospital on four days, 2–5 March (Old Style), and painted Mussorgsky in a hospital robe, red at the lapels and green in the folds; Mussorgsky died on 16 March (Old Style), 28 March in the modern calendar: https://my.tretyakov.ru/app/masterpiece/20705 (Russian). He was born on 9 (21) March 1839, and Khubov places his death in the same hospital: http://mussorgsky.ru/hubov001.html and http://mussorgsky.ru/hubov009.html (Russian).

cues.title: D major after the sabbath
cues.text: Harp arpeggios and quiet wind chords bring the night to rest in D major. The strings return for the last soft chord, and the basses pluck their final D. The score leaves a fermata over the silence.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 65: harp arpeggios, final D major harmony, pizzicato low strings and final rest with fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bell holds D as the dance stops
transitions.to: D · A bell disperses the witches
transitions.how: The rushing strings descend and diminish. At Poco meno mosso, a bell tuned to D begins its slow tolling. The cellos pluck D beneath quiet violin tremolo; clarinets hold their chord while the flutes move in longer notes. The trombones, tuba, bass drum and cymbals are finished for the night.
transitions.evidence: Bessel score, p. 60, rehearsal W: descending strings, Campana in D, Poco meno mosso and the marked cessation of the heavy brass and percussion.

transitions.title: The clarinet sings over low D
transitions.from: D · A bell disperses the witches
transitions.to: Coda · Clarinet and flute at daybreak
transitions.how: The moving violin figures stop. At Meno mosso, tranquillo, a solo clarinet sings over divided violas, cellos and double basses, with D held low. Harp arpeggios answer the end of its phrase before a solo flute takes up the dawn music.
transitions.evidence: Bessel score, pp. 63–64, rehearsals Y–Z: the violin parts cease, clarinet and flute solos alternate over low D, and harp arpeggios connect the phrases.

source.title: Mussorgsky, Night on Bald Mountain, Rimsky-Korsakov’s concert version, full score (Bessel)
source.locator: Opening, p. 3; woodwind and string dances, pp. 14–36; bell and dispersal at W, p. 60; clarinet and flute solos at Y–Z, p. 64; D major close, p. 65.

timeline.note: The two violin sections begin alone, pianissimo, in running figures.
Short woodwind and string phrases alternate with brass answers.
Piccolo and flutes race above the strings and the orchestra’s separated chords.
Long wind phrases sound above repeated muted-violin figures and plucked low strings.
Quick strings and woodwinds meet the returning brass summons.
Winds and strings repeat short figures before the brass answer again.
Upper winds and violins rush above brass chords and percussion.
The bell tolls D above quiet violin tremolo and plucked cellos.
Slow wind phrases sound above muted violins and sustained low strings.
The solo clarinet sings over divided violas and low strings; harp arpeggios answer its phrase.
The solo flute sings dolce above divided violas, cellos and plucked double basses.
Quiet wind chords and harp arpeggios settle on D major; the strings return for the last chord.

composer.epithet: He could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who can no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate: close-fitting uniform, polished manners, well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later another hospital would provide his most familiar likeness: Repin’s painting of a man in a dressing gown, hair in disorder, eyes still alert. There is a great deal of music between those two rooms.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano; his nurse’s stories stirred the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he went to school in Saint Petersburg and studied piano with Anton Gerke. The School of Guards Cadets followed in 1852, then a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid to publish his first piano piece, a polka. The boy could play for a drawing room before he knew how an orchestra worked.
